title: The AI said yes
28 times in 100
heading: Put the lock in the code: why an AI's "no" is not access control
intro: Arize's test support agent refused every direct request to send data out, yet pulled a stranger's record in 28 of 100 runs until its tools were scoped to the signed-in customer. Here are the sources, plus the confused deputy, the 1988 idea behind it.
items: Arize: A web page talked our agent into leaking a stranger's data
Nancy Chauhan (Oct 2026): 98 of 98 direct requests refused, 28 of 100 routine-sounding lookups leaked, 0 leaks once every customer tool was bound to the logged-in session in code.
Sasi Levi: an ordinary email to a public support inbox got quarterly sales numbers back, because the AI workflow ran with its creator's privileges. No prompt injection needed.

One prompt to an exposed AWS Bedrock AgentCore agent reached the metadata service and returned credentials for a default role that spanned every AgentCore agent in the account's region. AWS hardened the role by Sept 29, 2026.
A denied agent fetched a routine approval token and completed the protected operation in 8 of 9 reruns: possession of a token was treated as permission.
MCP Security Best Practices: Confused Deputy Problem
The official MCP guidance on confused deputies and token passthrough: servers must not accept tokens that were not issued for them.
A builder and defender's guide released Nov 10, 2026, covering architecture, identity and access controls, runtime protection, supply chain, and testing.
